modules.title: 01. Java fundamentals
modules.description: Java runs a large share of backend systems in banks, e-commerce and product companies. Learn the language, collections, exceptions, builds and tests.

lessons.title: Java syntax, classes, records, interfaces and collections
objectives: Install a JDK (21 LTS) and compile and run programs.
Write classes, records, interfaces and enums.
Use List, Map, Set and the streams API.

topics.title: Language basics
details: Static typing, `var` for local inference, classes with constructors and methods, access modifiers (private by default in practice).

topics.title: Modern Java
details: Records for immutable data (`record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency)`), sealed interfaces, switch expressions and pattern matching.

topics.title: Collections and streams
details: ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet; `orders.stream().filter(Order::paid).mapToLong(Order::total).sum()`; never use double for money, use BigDecimal or long minor units.

reading.locator: dev.java Learn: 'Getting Started with Java', 'Language Basics', 'Classes and Objects', 'Records', 'Interfaces' and 'The Collections Framework'.

assignment.title: Banking domain in Java
instructions: Model Account, Money (record) and Transfer with rules: no negative balances, same currency only.
Use collections and streams to compute statements per account.
Throw specific exceptions for rule violations.
acceptanceCriteria: Money uses BigDecimal or long minor units, never double.
Rule violations raise clear exceptions.

questions.prompt: Why not use double for money?
questions.answer: Binary floating point cannot represent many decimal amounts exactly.
questions.explanation: Use BigDecimal or integer minor units.

questions.prompt: What is a Java record?
questions.answer: A concise immutable data class with generated equals, hashCode and toString.

reviewPrompts: Write a stream that groups orders by customer.

lessons.title: Exceptions, Maven/Gradle builds and JUnit testing
objectives: Use checked and unchecked exceptions appropriately.
Structure a Maven or Gradle project with dependencies.
Write JUnit 5 tests including parameterised tests.

topics.title: Exceptions
details: Checked exceptions must be declared; unchecked (RuntimeException) are for programming errors. Never swallow exceptions silently; add context.

topics.title: Builds
details: Maven: pom.xml, src/main/java, src/test/java, `mvn test`, `mvn package`; Gradle is an alternative with build.gradle.

topics.title: Testing
details: `@Test`, assertions, `@ParameterizedTest` for many cases, AssertJ for readable assertions.

reading.locator: JUnit 5 user guide: 'Overview', 'Writing Tests' (annotations, assertions, display names) and 'Parameterized Tests'.

assignment.title: Test the banking domain
instructions: Convert your project to Maven or Gradle.
Write 20+ JUnit tests including parameterised tests for transfer rules.
Add GitHub Actions running the tests.
acceptanceCriteria: CI passes; tests cover every rule including failure paths.

questions.prompt: Checked vs unchecked exceptions?
questions.answer: Checked must be declared or handled; unchecked (RuntimeException) need not.

questions.prompt: Maven test sources folder?
questions.answer: src/test/java.

reviewPrompts: When would you create a custom exception?

modules.title: 02. Spring Boot services
modules.description: The most common Java backend framework. Build REST APIs with dependency injection, validation, persistence and integration tests.

lessons.title: REST controllers, dependency injection and configuration
objectives: Create a Spring Boot app and expose REST endpoints.
Explain dependency injection and bean lifecycles.
Use configuration properties, profiles and actuator health checks.

topics.title: Controllers
details: `@RestController` with `@GetMapping`/`@PostMapping`; request bodies map to records; `@Valid` with constraints returns 400 on bad input.

topics.title: Dependency injection
details: Spring creates beans and injects them through constructors, so classes depend on interfaces and tests can supply fakes.

topics.title: Configuration
details: application.yml, profiles (dev/test/prod), environment variables for secrets; actuator exposes /health and metrics.

reading.locator: Spring guide 'Building a RESTful Web Service' in full, then the Spring Boot reference sections on 'Externalized Configuration' and 'Profiles'.

assignment.title: Accounts API
instructions: Build a Spring Boot accounts API (create account, get account, list) with validation and a global error handler.
Use constructor injection and an in-memory repository behind an interface.
Add actuator health and a dev profile.
acceptanceCriteria: Bad input returns 400 with a consistent error body.

questions.prompt: Why constructor injection?
questions.answer: Dependencies are explicit, final and easy to replace in tests.

questions.prompt: Where should secrets come from in Spring Boot?
questions.answer: Environment variables or a secret manager, not committed config files.

lessons.title: Persistence with JPA, transactions and Testcontainers
objectives: Map entities and repositories with Spring Data JPA.
Use @Transactional correctly and avoid N+1 queries.
Run integration tests against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers.

topics.title: JPA
details: Entities map to tables; repositories give CRUD; use migrations (Flyway/Liquibase) instead of auto-DDL in real projects.

topics.title: Transactions
details: @Transactional on service methods makes their database work atomic; it only works on public methods called through the Spring proxy.

topics.title: Performance and tests
details: Loading a list then touching lazy relations per row causes N+1 queries; use fetch joins. Testcontainers starts PostgreSQL in Docker for tests.

reading.locator: Spring guide 'Accessing Data with JPA', then the Testcontainers 'Quickstart' for JUnit 5.

assignment.title: Persistent transfers
instructions: Persist accounts and transfers in PostgreSQL with Flyway migrations.
Implement a transactional transfer service; prove a failure mid-transfer rolls back.
Write Testcontainers integration tests and fix an N+1 query you introduce on purpose.
deliverables: Project with migrations and integration tests.
acceptanceCriteria: Rollback test passes against real PostgreSQL.
Query count drops after fixing N+1.

questions.prompt: What is the N+1 query problem?
questions.answer: Loading N rows and then running one extra query per row for related data.
questions.explanation: Fix with joins or fetch joins.

questions.prompt: Why test with a real database instead of an in-memory fake?
questions.answer: Real SQL, constraints and locking behaviour differ from fakes.

modules.title: 03. Building HTTP services in Go
modules.description: Go's standard library is enough to build fast, production-grade HTTP services. Learn handlers, middleware, graceful shutdown and database access.

lessons.title: net/http, middleware, JSON, databases and graceful shutdown
objectives: Write handlers with net/http and route with the standard ServeMux patterns.
Add middleware for logging, request IDs and timeouts.
Access PostgreSQL with pgx and shut down gracefully.

topics.title: Handlers
details: A handler writes a response for a request; decode JSON with limits (http.MaxBytesReader) and validate; return proper status codes.

topics.title: Middleware
details: Wrap handlers to add logging, request IDs, auth and per-request timeouts with context.

topics.title: Production basics
details: Set server read/write timeouts; use a connection pool (pgxpool); on SIGTERM stop accepting requests and finish in-flight ones (Server.Shutdown).

reading.locator: Go article 'Writing Web Applications' in full; then Effective Go's section on concurrency for request handling.

assignment.title: Jobs API in Go
instructions: Build a Go HTTP API to create and query jobs stored in PostgreSQL (pgx).
Add logging and request-ID middleware, request timeouts and graceful shutdown.
Write handler tests with httptest and integration tests with a containerised database.
deliverables: Go service with tests and Dockerfile.
acceptanceCriteria: Graceful shutdown finishes in-flight requests in a test.
Oversized bodies are rejected.

questions.prompt: Why set server timeouts in Go?
questions.answer: Without them slow clients can hold connections forever.

questions.prompt: What does graceful shutdown do?
questions.answer: Stops accepting new requests and lets in-flight requests finish.

reviewPrompts: How do you pass a request ID through calls?

modules.title: 04. PostgreSQL for backend engineers
modules.description: Correctness under concurrency: isolation levels, locking strategies, indexes for real queries and safe schema migrations.

lessons.title: Isolation levels, row locks, optimistic locking and deadlocks
objectives: Explain read committed, repeatable read and serializable in PostgreSQL.
Choose pessimistic (SELECT FOR UPDATE) or optimistic (version column) locking.
Diagnose and avoid deadlocks.

topics.title: Isolation
details: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed; repeatable read uses a snapshot; serializable detects anomalies and aborts one transaction, so clients must retry.

topics.title: Locking strategies
details: Pessimistic: lock rows you will update. Optimistic: `UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` and retry if zero rows changed.

topics.title: Deadlocks
details: Lock rows in a consistent order (e.g. by account ID) and keep transactions short.

video.locator: CMU 15-445 lectures on concurrency control (two-phase locking and MVCC).

reading.locator: PostgreSQL manual chapter 13 'Concurrency Control': 13.2 'Transaction Isolation' and 13.3 'Explicit Locking' (row-level locks and deadlocks).

assignment.title: Concurrent transfers lab
instructions: Write a test that runs 1,000 concurrent transfers between 10 accounts and checks the total balance is unchanged.
Implement pessimistic and optimistic versions; compare throughput and retry counts.
Create a deadlock, then fix it with consistent lock ordering.
deliverables: Code, results table and deadlock notes.
acceptanceCriteria: Total balance is preserved in both versions.
Deadlock is reproduced and fixed.

questions.prompt: What must clients do under SERIALIZABLE isolation?
questions.answer: Retry transactions that fail with serialization errors.
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL aborts one of the conflicting transactions.

questions.prompt: How does optimistic locking detect conflicts?
questions.answer: A version column that must match when updating.
questions.explanation: Zero updated rows means someone else changed it.

lessons.title: Indexes for real queries, EXPLAIN and zero-downtime migrations
objectives: Design composite and partial indexes for actual query patterns.
Use EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) to verify plans.
Run schema migrations without downtime.

topics.title: Indexes
details: Composite index order matters: (customer_id, created_at) serves 'orders for a customer, newest first'. Partial indexes cover hot subsets (WHERE status = 'pending').

topics.title: Plans
details: Compare estimated and actual rows; watch for sequential scans on big tables and sorts spilling to disk.

topics.title: Safe migrations
details: Add nullable columns first, backfill in batches, then add constraints; `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` avoids blocking writes; expand-and-contract for renames.

reading.locator: PostgreSQL manual: chapter 11 'Indexes' (multicolumn, partial and index-only scans) and 14.1 'Using EXPLAIN'; CREATE INDEX reference section 'Building Indexes Concurrently'.

assignment.title: Index a slow endpoint
instructions: Load 5 million orders; find the slowest endpoint query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
Add the right composite or partial index and measure.
Write an expand-and-contract migration plan to rename a column with no downtime.
deliverables: Plans before/after, timings and migration plan.
acceptanceCriteria: Measured speed-up with the plan change shown.

questions.prompt: Why does column order matter in a composite index?
questions.answer: The index is sorted by the first column, then the next.
questions.explanation: Queries must use the leading columns.

questions.prompt: How do you add an index without blocking writes?
questions.answer: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY.
questions.explanation: Takes longer but avoids long locks.

reviewPrompts: Design an index for 'pending jobs ordered by run_at'.

modules.title: 05. Caching with Redis
modules.description: Make reads fast without serving wrong data: cache-aside, TTLs, invalidation, stampedes and Redis data structures.

lessons.title: Cache-aside, TTLs, invalidation, stampedes and rate limiting
objectives: Implement cache-aside with TTLs and invalidation on writes.
Prevent cache stampedes and handle Redis being down.
Use Redis data structures for counters, leaderboards and rate limits.

topics.title: Patterns
details: Cache-aside: read cache, on miss read DB and set cache with TTL; on write update DB then delete the cache key.

topics.title: Failure modes
details: Stampede: many requests miss at once and hit the DB; use request coalescing or jittered TTLs. If Redis is down, fall back to the DB with protection.

topics.title: Structures
details: Strings with INCR for counters, sorted sets for leaderboards, hashes for objects; token-bucket rate limiting with a Lua script for atomicity.

reading.locator: Database Caching Strategies Using Redis: 'Caching patterns' (cache-aside, write-through), 'Cache validity' and 'Evictions'.

assignment.title: Cache a product API
instructions: Add cache-aside to your Spring Boot or Go service for a product lookup.
Load-test with and without the cache; simulate a stampede and fix it.
Add a Redis token-bucket rate limiter returning 429 with Retry-After.
acceptanceCriteria: Writes invalidate the cache (test proves no stale reads after update).
Rate limiter is atomic under concurrency.

questions.prompt: In cache-aside, what happens on a write?
questions.answer: Update the database, then delete the cache entry.

questions.prompt: What is a cache stampede?
questions.answer: Many requests miss simultaneously and overload the database.

modules.title: 06. Event-driven services with Kafka
modules.description: Decouple services with events: publishing, consuming, ordering, retries, dead-letter topics and schema evolution.

lessons.title: Producers, consumers, retries, dead-letter topics and event schemas
objectives: Publish and consume events from a Spring Boot or Go service.
Handle retries, poison messages and dead-letter topics.
Version event schemas safely.

topics.title: Basics for services
details: Key events by entity ID for per-entity ordering; consumers in a group share partitions; commit offsets after successful processing.

topics.title: Failures
details: Consumers must be idempotent (events can arrive twice). Retry transient errors with backoff; send messages that keep failing to a dead-letter topic with the error.

topics.title: Schemas
details: Define events with explicit schemas (JSON Schema, Avro, Protobuf); only add optional fields; include event ID, type, version and time.

reading.locator: Kafka 'Introduction' in full, then the main documentation's 'Design' section on message delivery semantics.

assignment.title: Order events
instructions: Publish OrderPlaced events from your service; build a separate notification consumer.
Make the consumer idempotent with a processed-events table.
Add retries with backoff and a dead-letter topic; demonstrate with a poison message.
deliverables: Two services, compose file and a failure demo.
acceptanceCriteria: Duplicate events cause no duplicate notifications.
Poison messages land in the DLT.

questions.prompt: Why must Kafka consumers be idempotent?
questions.answer: Events can be delivered more than once.
questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery is the common default.

questions.prompt: What is a dead-letter topic for?
questions.answer: Holding messages that keep failing so they do not block processing.
questions.explanation: They can be inspected and replayed.

reviewPrompts: How do you keep per-order event ordering?
What fields does every event need?

modules.title: 07. Reliable distributed transactions
modules.description: Money and orders must never be lost or duplicated. Learn idempotency keys, the transactional outbox and sagas.

lessons.title: Idempotency keys and double-entry ledgers
objectives: Implement idempotency keys for POST endpoints.
Model money movement with double-entry accounting.
Prove no money is created or lost under retries and concurrency.

topics.title: Idempotency keys
details: The client sends a unique key; the server stores the key with the request hash and response; a repeat returns the stored response; a different body with the same key is rejected.

topics.title: Double entry
details: Every transfer writes balanced postings (debit one account, credit another); the sum of all postings is always zero, so errors are detectable.

topics.title: Verification
details: Randomised tests with retries and concurrency, then reconcile balances from postings.

reading.locator: Stripe 'Idempotent requests' page in full; then design your own storage table for keys.

assignment.title: Ledger core
instructions: Build a transfer endpoint backed by journal entries and postings with an idempotency-key table.
Run 100,000 randomised transfers with injected retries and duplicate requests.
Reconcile: every entry sums to zero and balances equal postings.
acceptanceCriteria: Zero drift across all runs.
Same key + different body returns 409.

questions.prompt: What does an idempotency key let a client do?
questions.answer: Safely retry a request without duplicating its effect.
questions.explanation: The server returns the original result.

questions.prompt: Invariant of double-entry accounting?
questions.answer: Debits and credits of every entry sum to zero.

lessons.title: The transactional outbox and sagas
objectives: Explain the dual-write problem.
Implement a transactional outbox with a relay to Kafka.
Coordinate multi-service workflows with sagas and compensations.

topics.title: Dual writes
details: Writing to the database and publishing an event separately can leave them inconsistent if the process crashes in between.

topics.title: Outbox
details: Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change; a relay publishes outbox rows and marks them sent (at least once).

topics.title: Sagas
details: A long workflow is a sequence of local transactions; if a later step fails, run compensating actions (refund, release stock). Orchestrated or choreographed.

reading.locator: microservices.io 'Transactional outbox' pattern page; then the 'Saga' pattern page linked from it.

assignment.title: Outbox and a saga
instructions: Add an outbox table and relay to your ledger; kill the app between commit and publish and show the event is still delivered.
Implement an order saga (reserve stock -> charge -> confirm) with compensations on failure.
deliverables: Code, crash test and saga failure demo.
acceptanceCriteria: No lost events after crashes.
Failed charges trigger stock release.

questions.prompt: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
questions.answer: Keeping database changes and published events consistent without distributed transactions.
questions.explanation: Both are written in one local transaction.

questions.prompt: What is a compensating action?
questions.answer: An action that semantically undoes a completed saga step, such as a refund.
questions.explanation: Used when a later step fails.

modules.title: 08. Background jobs and scheduling
modules.description: Run work outside the request path: job queues in PostgreSQL, retries with backoff, dead letters, cron schedules and leader election.

lessons.title: Job queues with SKIP LOCKED, retries, dead letters and leader election
objectives: Build a job queue on PostgreSQL with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
Implement retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and dead-lettering.
Run cron schedules exactly once with a single leader using advisory locks.

topics.title: Queue
details: Workers claim jobs with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT n`, so no two workers take the same job; leases with heartbeats recover jobs from crashed workers.

topics.title: Retries
details: Backoff = base x 2^attempt with random jitter; after max attempts mark the job dead with the last error.

topics.title: Scheduling
details: Only the leader enqueues cron runs; `pg_try_advisory_lock` elects a leader; a unique constraint on (schedule, run_time) prevents duplicates even if two leaders overlap.

reading.locator: PostgreSQL manual: SELECT reference section 'The Locking Clause' (SKIP LOCKED) and 13.3.5 'Advisory Locks'.

assignment.title: Go job scheduler
instructions: Build a Go scheduler with an API, workers using SKIP LOCKED, leases and retries with jitter.
Add cron schedules with advisory-lock leader election and a uniqueness guard.
Fault tests: kill workers and the leader; prove no job is lost or run twice by the scheduler.
deliverables: Code, fault-test results and dashboard plan.
acceptanceCriteria: Two scheduler replicas never enqueue the same cron run twice.

questions.prompt: What does SKIP LOCKED do?
questions.answer: Skips rows locked by other transactions instead of waiting.
questions.explanation: Lets many workers pull jobs concurrently.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to retry backoff?
questions.answer: To avoid many clients retrying at the same moment.

reviewPrompts: How does the uniqueness guard back up leader election?

modules.title: 09. Observability: metrics, logs and traces
modules.description: Know what your service is doing in production: structured logs, Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, dashboards and alerts.

lessons.title: Metrics with Prometheus, structured logs and traces with OpenTelemetry
objectives: Instrument RED metrics (rate, errors, duration) with histograms.
Write structured JSON logs with request and trace IDs.
Trace a request across services with OpenTelemetry.

topics.title: Metrics
details: Counters for requests and errors, histograms for latency (so you can compute p95/p99), gauges for queue depth; avoid high-cardinality labels like user IDs.

topics.title: Logs
details: Structured JSON with level, message, request_id, trace_id; never log secrets or personal data.

topics.title: Traces
details: A trace is a tree of spans showing where time went across services; propagate context in HTTP headers.

reading.locator: Prometheus 'Instrumentation' best practices page in full, then 'Histograms and summaries'.

assignment.title: Instrument two services
instructions: Add Prometheus metrics (RED + business metrics) and structured logs to two of your services.
Add OpenTelemetry tracing across a call between them; view traces in Jaeger or Grafana Tempo.
Find a deliberately slow database call using the trace.
deliverables: Instrumented code, compose stack and screenshots.
acceptanceCriteria: p95 latency is computed from histograms.
One trace spans both services.

questions.prompt: Why use histograms for latency?
questions.answer: They let you compute percentiles like p95 and p99 across instances.

questions.prompt: Why avoid user IDs as metric labels?
questions.answer: High cardinality explodes storage and query cost.
questions.explanation: Put them in logs or traces instead.

lessons.title: Dashboards, SLOs and alerting that people trust
objectives: Define SLIs and SLOs and compute an error budget.
Build Grafana dashboards for a service.
Write symptom-based alerts with runbooks.

topics.title: SLOs
details: SLI: measured indicator (fraction of requests under 300 ms). SLO: target (99.5% over 30 days). Error budget: the allowed 0.5%.

topics.title: Dashboards
details: Top row: traffic, errors, latency, saturation; then dependencies; link to logs and traces.

topics.title: Alerts
details: Alert on user-visible symptoms and fast error-budget burn, not every CPU spike; every alert has an owner and a runbook.

reading.locator: Google SRE book chapter 4 'Service Level Objectives' in full.

assignment.title: SLO for your API
instructions: Define two SLIs and SLOs for one service; build a Grafana dashboard.
Write a burn-rate alert in Prometheus and a runbook for it.
Trigger it with injected errors and follow the runbook.
deliverables: Dashboard JSON, alert rules, runbook and drill notes.
acceptanceCriteria: The alert fires on injected errors and the runbook resolves it.

questions.prompt: What is an error budget?
questions.answer: The amount of unreliability an SLO allows, e.g. 0.5% of requests.

questions.prompt: What should alerts be based on?
questions.answer: User-visible symptoms and SLO burn.

modules.title: 10. Performance and load testing
modules.description: Prove how much traffic your service handles: realistic load tests, latency percentiles, bottleneck hunting and capacity planning.

lessons.title: Load testing with k6, percentiles and finding bottlenecks
objectives: Write k6 scripts with realistic traffic and thresholds.
Interpret throughput and p50/p95/p99 latency.
Find and fix the bottleneck (database, locks, pool size, CPU).

topics.title: Workload
details: Model realistic mixes (80% reads, 20% writes), think time and data; ramp up gradually; run long enough to see steady state.

topics.title: Reading results
details: Throughput plateaus while latency rises when you hit a bottleneck; check pool waits, slow queries, lock waits and CPU.

topics.title: Capacity
details: Record the knee point, then plan capacity with headroom (e.g. 2x expected peak).

reading.locator: k6 docs: 'Get started' (write and run your first test), 'Thresholds', 'Scenarios' and 'Results output'.

assignment.title: Find the knee
instructions: Write a k6 test for your ledger API with a realistic mix and thresholds (p95 < 200 ms, errors < 1%).
Ramp until thresholds fail; identify the bottleneck with your metrics and traces.
Fix one bottleneck and re-run; report before/after.
deliverables: k6 scripts, results and bottleneck analysis.
acceptanceCriteria: Reported numbers name the hardware and configuration.

questions.prompt: What signals a bottleneck in a load test?
questions.answer: Throughput stops rising while latency climbs.

questions.prompt: Why test with realistic traffic mixes?
questions.answer: Bottlenecks depend on the mix of reads and writes.

reviewPrompts: How much headroom would you plan for?

modules.title: 11. API security and resilience
modules.description: Protect and harden APIs: OAuth2/JWT, authorisation checks, rate limiting, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and graceful degradation.

lessons.title: OAuth 2.0, JWT and authorisation done right
objectives: Explain OAuth 2.0 flows and OpenID Connect at a practical level.
Validate JWTs correctly (signature, issuer, audience, expiry).
Enforce object-level authorisation on every endpoint.

topics.title: OAuth/OIDC
details: OAuth 2.0 delegates access with tokens; OIDC adds identity (ID token). Use the authorization code flow with PKCE for user apps; client credentials for service-to-service.

topics.title: JWT
details: Verify the signature with the issuer's keys, check iss, aud, exp; never accept 'alg: none'; keep tokens short-lived.

topics.title: Authorisation
details: Check that the caller may access this specific object on every request (prevents broken object-level authorisation, the top API risk).

reading.locator: OWASP Cheat Sheet Series: 'JSON Web Token for Java Cheat Sheet' and 'Authorization Cheat Sheet'.

assignment.title: Secure the accounts API
instructions: Protect your Spring Boot API as an OAuth2 resource server using a local Keycloak (Docker) issuer.
Enforce that users can access only their own accounts; write tests for cross-user access.
Test expired, wrong-audience and tampered tokens.
deliverables: Secured service, Keycloak setup and tests.
acceptanceCriteria: All negative token tests are rejected with 401/403.

questions.prompt: Which OAuth flow for a web or mobile user app?
questions.answer: Authorization code with PKCE.

questions.prompt: What must you verify on a JWT?
questions.answer: Signature, issuer, audience and expiry.

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and graceful degradation
objectives: Set timeouts on every remote call and budget them across a request.
Retry safely with backoff and jitter, only for idempotent operations.
Use circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks to contain failures.

topics.title: Timeouts
details: A call without a timeout can hang threads forever; set per-call timeouts smaller than the caller's overall deadline.

topics.title: Retries
details: Retry only transient failures, with capped exponential backoff and jitter, and only idempotent operations (or with idempotency keys).

topics.title: Containment
details: Circuit breakers stop calling a failing dependency for a while; bulkheads isolate thread pools; fallbacks serve cached or partial data.

reading.locator: Amazon Builders' Library 'Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter' in full.

assignment.title: Chaos on a dependency
instructions: Put a slow/failing fake dependency behind your service (toxiproxy or a test server).
Add timeouts, retries with jitter and a circuit breaker (Resilience4j or your own in Go).
Show latency and error rates with and without protections during the failure.
acceptanceCriteria: With protections, the service stays responsive during dependency failure.

questions.prompt: Why add jitter to retries?
questions.answer: To spread retries out and avoid synchronized retry storms.

questions.prompt: What does a circuit breaker do?
questions.answer: Stops calling a failing dependency for a period and fails fast.

modules.title: 12. Backend system design
modules.description: Put it all together: design a backend system end to end and defend the choices, as in senior backend interviews.

lessons.title: Designing a payments platform end to end
objectives: Design APIs, data model, consistency, messaging and failure handling for payments.
Explain how the design prevents double charges and lost money.
Plan observability, security and capacity for it.

topics.title: Core flows
details: Create payment intent (idempotent), authorise with a provider, capture, refund; ledger entries for every money movement; reconciliation with provider reports daily.

topics.title: Consistency
details: Strong consistency inside the ledger database; events via outbox; sagas for multi-step flows; webhooks from providers handled idempotently.

topics.title: Operations
details: SLOs on authorisation latency and success rate, alerts on reconciliation mismatches, PCI scope minimised by never storing card numbers.

reading.locator: System Design Primer: revisit 'Consistency patterns', 'Availability patterns' and 'Asynchronism' with payments in mind; then apply the interview framework.

assignment.title: Payments design doc
instructions: Write a 4-page design doc for a payments platform for an Indian e-commerce company (UPI and cards via a provider).
Include API, data model, sequence diagrams for pay and refund, failure scenarios and reconciliation.
Present it in a 20-minute mock design interview.
acceptanceCriteria: Every failure scenario names the mechanism that prevents money loss or duplication.

questions.prompt: How do you prevent double charges when a client retries?
questions.answer: Idempotency keys on payment creation.
questions.explanation: The provider call is also made idempotent.

questions.prompt: Why reconcile with provider reports?
questions.answer: To detect mismatches between your ledger and actual money movements.

limitations: Skill-builder lessons are beginner-first: each one assumes you have not used the tool before and explains the vocabulary before the practice.
Readings are official documentation or free books, linked rather than copied. Check the current version when you open a link; tools change.
Use your own machine, free tiers and synthetic or public data. Never use employer code, client data or credentials in exercises.
